title: Si apruebo, te invito
titleEn: If I pass, dinner's on me
blurbEn: Conditions that might really happen — and the one thing Spanish will not let you put after 'si'.
body:
El examen es el sábado que viene y llevo dos semanas durmiendo mal.

Si apruebo, invito a toda la clase a cenar. Lo he prometido delante de testigos, así que ya no hay marcha atrás.

Si suspendo, me lo tomaré con calma y me presentaré en septiembre. Eso también lo he dicho, aunque con bastante menos entusiasmo.

Las condiciones reales en español son sencillas: «si» más presente, y después futuro o presente. Si llueve, no salgo. Si tengo tiempo, te llamo. Si apruebo, invito a todos.

Lo único que no se puede hacer es poner el futuro detrás de «si». «Si aprobaré» no existe. En inglés tampoco, aunque nadie lo explica nunca.

Diego dice que si invito a cenar a doce personas voy a necesitar aprobar y un préstamo.

Tiene razón, como siempre. Y como siempre, no pienso hacerle caso.
translationEn:
The exam is next Saturday and I've been sleeping badly for two weeks.

If I pass, I'm taking the whole class out to dinner. I've promised it in front of witnesses, so there's no going back now.

If I fail, I'll take it calmly and sit it again in September. I've said that too, though with considerably less enthusiasm.

Real conditions in Spanish are simple: "si" plus the present, then the future or the present. If it rains, I don't go out. If I have time, I'll call you. If I pass, I'm buying dinner.

The one thing you can't do is put the future after "si". "Si aprobaré" doesn't exist. It doesn't in English either, though nobody ever explains that.

Diego says that if I take twelve people out to dinner I'm going to need to pass and a loan.

He's right, as always. And as always, I don't intend to listen.

Si apruebo.note: Present tense after 'si', even though it clearly refers to the future. This is the rule the whole text turns on.

invito.note: The main clause can be present or future. The present sounds more certain, almost like a promise.
